content: Infuse 1 liter of fluids within 15–20 minutes as quickly as possible. If necessary, repeat the infusion.g., puffiness). If breathing difficulty or puffiness develops, reduce the rate further to 5 ml/min. Monitor urine output and record the time and amount of fluids administered. For conditions such as severe abdominal pain, obstructed labor, ectopic pregnancy, dangerous fever, or dehydration, administer fluids at a moderate rate, infusing 1 liter over 2–3 hours. In cases of severe anemia, pre-eclampsia, or eclampsia, administer fluids at a slow rate, infusing 1 liter over 6–8 hours. If intravenous access is not possible, provide oral rehydration solution (ORS) if the woman can drink, or administer it via a nasogastric tube. Give 300–500 ml of ORS over 1 hour. Do not give ORS to unconscious women or those experiencing convulsions. If heavy postpartum bleeding persists after delivery of the placenta or if the uterus is soft and not well-contracted, place a cupped palm on the uterine fundus to assess contraction. Massage the fundus in a circular motion until the uterus becomes firm. Once the uterus is well-contracted, use your fingers to push down behind the fundus in one swift motion to expel clots. If heavy postpartum bleeding continues despite uterine massage, oxytocin or ergometrine treatment, and removal of the placenta, apply bimanual uterine compression. Wear sterile gloves, insert your right hand into the vagina with a clenched fist, and place the other hand on the abdomen behind the uterus. Firmly compress the uterus between both hands until the bleeding stops. If bleeding persists, apply aortic compression by pressing above the umbilicus to stop blood flow. Administer oxytocin for heavy postpartum bleeding. The initial dose is 10 IU intramuscularly (IM) or intravenously (IV). If bleeding persists after 20 minutes, repeat the dose. For IV infusion, administer 20 IU in 1 liter of fluid at 60 drops per minute, or 10 IU in 1 liter at 30 drops per minute. Do not exceed 3 liters of IV fluids containing oxytocin. If IV oxytocin is unavailable or ineffective, administer misoprostol (800 µg) sublingually. If bleeding continues after oxytocin, administer ergometrine (0.2 mg IM), but do not use it in cases of eclampsia, pre-eclampsia, hypertension, or retained placenta. If the placenta is not delivered within 1 hour after childbirth or if heavy vaginal bleeding persists despite uterine massage and oxytocin, manually remove the placenta. Explain the procedure to the woman and obtain her consent. Insert an IV line and administer fluids rapidly if bleeding is present or slowly if not. Wash hands and forearms thoroughly, wear long sterile gloves, and clean the vulva and perineal area. To remove the placenta, hold the umbilical cord with a clamp using your left hand and gently pull it horizontally. Insert your right hand into the vagina and up into the uterus. Support the uterine fundus with your left hand to provide counter-traction. Use the fingers of your right hand to locate the edge of the placenta and detach it from the uterine wall by gradually creating a space between the placenta and the uterine wall. Continue this process around the entire placental bed until the placenta is fully detached. Gradually withdraw your hand, bringing the placenta with it. Examine the placenta to confirm it is complete. If any fragments are missing, re-explore the uterine cavity to remove them. If the placenta does not separate easily or if a constriction ring or closed cervix prevents access, do not persist. Refer the woman urgently to a hospital. After manual removal of the placenta, administer 10 IU of oxytocin IM/IV and massage the uterine fundus to encourage contraction. Provide antibiotic prophylaxis with a single dose of ampicillin (2 g IV/IM). If bleeding stops, administer fluids slowly for at least 1 hour. If it is not, massage the uterus and repeat oxytocin administration. For eclampsia or severe pre-eclampsia, administer magnesium sulfate as a loading dose. Insert an IV line and give fluids slowly (1 liter over 6–8 hours). Administer 4 g of magnesium sulfate (20 ml of a 20% solution) IV slowly over 20 minutes, followed by 10 g IM (5 g in each buttock with 1 ml of 2% lignocaine). If IV access is unavailable, administer 10 g IM only. If convulsions recur, administer an additional 2 g of magnesium sulfate IV over 20 minutes. If convulsions persist, administer diazepam. Continue magnesium sulfate treatment every 4 hours (5 g IM in alternate buttocks) until 24 hours after delivery or the last convulsion. Monitor urine output, respiratory rate, and knee reflexes before administering the next dose. Do not administer magnesium sulfate if the knee reflex is absent, urine output is less than 100 ml in 4 hours, or respiratory rate is below 16 breaths per minute. If respiratory depression occurs, administer calcium gluconate (1 g IV over 10 minutes). For infections, administer appropriate IV/IM antibiotics before referral. If referral is delayed, continue antibiotics for 48 hours after the woman is fever-free, then switch to oral amoxicillin (500 mg three times daily) to complete 7 days of treatment. If signs of infection persist or the woman becomes weak or experiences abdominal pain postpartum, refer her urgently to a hospital. For malaria in pregnancy, confirm the diagnosis with parasitological testing. Administer the loading dose of the most effective antimalarial drug according to national guidelines. If artesunate or quinine is used, divide the dose into two injections, one in each anterior thigh. Always administer glucose with quinine. Refer the woman urgently to a hospital. If delivery is imminent or referral is delayed, continue treatment and refer after delivery. If she is unconscious, position her on her back with her head tilted backward and chin lifted to open the airway. Clear any obstructions or secretions from the throat. Insert an IV line and administer fluids as needed. If referral is necessary, provide emergency treatment before transport, organize transportation, and accompany the woman if possible.
